consensus_summary: Across all four blind responses the primary meaning is the valley as a season or place of trial, suffering, spiritual darkness, or danger through which God accompanies the believer, contrasted with the mountaintop (anchored in Psalm 23:4). Recognized secondary strands: divine judgment/decision (Joel 3), humility/lowliness exalted by God (Isa 40:4; Luke 3:5), restoration and resurrection hope (Ezek 37; Hos 2:15), and fertility/blessing (minority). One response notes scholarship treats valleys contextually rather than by a single code.
book_summary: The book identifies the valley as the low, humbled passage between mountain-kingdoms: the Way of descent, service, and obedience even unto death by which one leaves one rule and ascends another. A valley lifted or filled pictures resurrection, exaltation, and the preparation of the Way into the Mountain of God — with Mountain as its explicit opposite. It flags the common teaching (low seasons of trial and death versus the mountaintop) as the 'commonly taught' view distinct from its own.
consensus_core_identification: Valley = the low place/season of trial, suffering, and death-shadow that the believer passes through with God's presence, opposite the mountaintop of blessing and revelation.
book_core_identification: Valley = the Way of voluntary descent, humble service, and obedience unto death that carries one out from under one mountain-rule toward another; its filling/lifting signifies resurrection, exaltation, and preparation of the Way of the Lord.
boundary_disagreement: The book reclassifies the valley from a passively endured season of affliction into an active, purposive Way of kenotic descent and obedience (Phil 2:5-9) that terminates in exaltation. It adds cases the consensus does not center: the valley as transit between two competing rules/kingdoms (1 Sam 17:3, 8-9, where the outcome determines whose servants the people become), and the filled valley as the prepared Way into God's Mountain. It demotes the generic 'trial/dark season' reading — the consensus primary — to the 'commonly taught' view, effectively excluding mere hardship-without-obedient-descent from the symbol's core. The consensus's humility-exalted alternative (Isa 40:4; Luke 3:5) and resurrection strand (Ezek 37) are absorbed and promoted to the center.
rationale: The book does not replace the consensus referent outright: the valley remains the low place set against the mountain, and its central content — lowliness, death, and subsequent lifting — is already present in the consensus as the 'common' humility-exalted alternative (Isa 40:3-4; Luke 3:4-6) and the restoration/resurrection strand (Ezek 37). But the book materially changes the boundary and precision: the valley is not a trial one suffers but a Way one walks in obedient descent between kingdoms, ending in exaltation. This is a real disagreement at the boundary (the consensus's primary 'season of trial' reading is sidelined as merely commonly taught), yet the general category — the humbled low place opposite the mountain, lifted by God — is intact. That fits REFINED with a compatible-overlap core and partial reclassification of the extension, not DIVERGENT, since both readings can be true of the same valleys in the same sense (the trial reading is subsumed rather than negated).
strongest_objection: One could argue for DIVERGENT: the book's common-view note explicitly sets its identification against the consensus primary ('low seasons of trial'), and its core — a purposive Way of obedience between kingdoms — is not any single consensus alternative but a synthetic construct; Philippians 2 never mentions a valley, and reading 1 Samuel 17's valley as symbolic transit between rules is an idiosyncratic move, so the center may be judged replaced rather than refined.
